claims.text: Controlled post-solidification aging that produces nanoscale second-phase particles can improve the strength–plasticity combination of refractory high-entropy alloys.
The starting as-solidified refractory alloy has a coarse or minimal precipitate distribution.
Post-solidification aging can nucleate and grow nanoscale second-phase precipitates.
L12 precipitates are a suitable coherently interfaced second phase for the proposed refractory alloy intervention.
Hf2Fe-type grain-boundary precipitates can be produced by aging a Ti-Zr-Hf-Nb-Ta-Fe refractory multi-principal-element alloy.
Aging between 500 and 700 °C for approximately 30 minutes to a few hours is an appropriate processing range for producing fine precipitates.
Careful control of aging can produce fine, discontinuous precipitates while avoiding continuous grain-boundary networks.
Optimally processed precipitates should have dimensions of approximately 4–10 nm.
The aging treatment will create a uniform precipitate distribution within the matrix and/or at grain boundaries.
Fine precipitates obstruct dislocation motion and thereby enhance strength.
The precipitates strengthen the alloy through Orowan bypass.
A controlled, discontinuous precipitate morphology minimizes stress-concentration sites and therefore leaves ductility largely unaffected.
The aged alloy will exhibit a yield-strength increase of approximately 10–20% or more relative to an as-solidified or non-aged reference.
The yield-strength increase will be accompanied by only a marginal reduction in ductility.
An as-solidified or non-precipitation-treated alloy is an appropriate reference for measuring the aging response.
Increasing aging temperature or duration beyond the optimum can increase precipitate volume fraction or produce a continuous precipitate network.
Continuous precipitate networks would increase strength at the expense of ductility.
The optimum aging temperature and duration depend on alloy composition and constituent-element diffusion kinetics.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis is explicitly restricted to treatments that retain nanoscale precipitates and avoid continuous networks, but the falsification rule treats formation of a coarse or continuous network as falsifying the mechanism. Such a result could instead show that the treatment fell outside the hypothesis's stated processing boundary.
